main_damage_causes: Erasure of prior relationship history between Mundungus and Harry, collapsing accumulated grievance and guilt into a comic first-meeting, which strips his eventual confrontation scenes of personal weight

Consistent comedic deflation of Mundungus's cowardice — pre-announcing it as a joke and surrounding his capture with Dobby comedy — prevents the audience from taking his moral failures (especially his abandonment leading to Mad-Eye's death) seriously as character statements

Omission of the Confundus/Snape revelation from the film corpus, which removes the only moment that gives Mundungus hidden structural significance and recontextualises his role as an unwitting instrument of Dumbledore's plan

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Seven Potters briefing) — Mundungus's self-introduction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book corpus, Mundungus is already known to Harry before the Seven Potters mission (Book Scene 30-34: Harry has met him at Grimmauld Place, been apologised to by him, watched him smoke his pipe and eye the silver). He is a long-standing Order member with a prior relationship with Harry.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Mundungus introduces himself to Harry as if they have never met: 'Mundungus Fletcher, Mr. Potter. I've always been a huge admirer.' This plays as a comedic first-meeting moment.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes a prior relationship with history, guilt, and uncomfortable familiarity between Mundungus and Harry. The film resets this to a comic cold introduction, erasing the accumulated tension (Mundungus abandoning Harry to Dementors, apologising at Grimmauld Place, Harry's simmering resentment) and turning him into a throwaway gag character rather than someone Harry has genuine grievances with.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 (Seven Potters briefing) — 'Technically, I've been coerced'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 149 establishes Mundungus's reluctance ('I'm a soldier, I'd sooner be a protector') and Book Scene 201 shows his post-flight justification ('I never wanted to come along, no offense, mate, but I never volunteered to die for you'). His cowardice is real and consequential but expressed through action, not upfront comic declaration.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Mundungus announces his cowardice as a punchline before the mission even begins: 'Technically, I've been coerced.' This is played purely for laughs.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the books, Mundungus's cowardice is a damaging character flaw that costs Mad-Eye his life and carries moral weight. Pre-announcing it as a joke defuses that weight entirely. The audience is invited to laugh at his cowardice rather than later feel the consequences of it, which diminishes the impact of his abandonment during the flight and Mad-Eye's death.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (aftermath at Weasley house) — Bill's report on Mundungus's abandonment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 169-175 show the Order carefully working through what happened, with Bill arguing Mundungus probably panicked rather than betrayed them, and Ron concluding 'I've learned is not to trust that cowardly little squit, Mundungus.' Mundungus's Disapparation is treated as a serious moral failure and a cause of grief over Mad-Eye.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bill delivers the line 'Mundungus took one look at Voldemort and Disapparated' flatly, as a bare factual report. There is no further discussion of Mundungus, no moral reckoning, no defence of him, no anger directed at him specifically. The scene moves immediately to the question of the leak.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this moment to crystallise Mundungus's defining flaw — his cowardice — and attach it to real consequence (Mad-Eye's death). The film's flat delivery strips this of moral weight. Mundungus is neither defended nor condemned; he simply disappears from the conversation. This prevents the audience from understanding his abandonment as a character statement rather than a plot convenience.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Grimmauld Place kitchen interrogation) — Dobby's addition and tonal shift
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 192-229 depict a tense, focused interrogation: Harry pins Mundungus with his wand, Kreacher attacks him with a saucepan, and Harry systematically extracts information about the locket. The scene is charged with Harry's fury at Mundungus for stealing Sirius's things. Kreacher alone retrieves Mundungus (Book Scene 192).
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Dobby is added as a second captor, and his cheerful self-explanation ('Dobby saw Kreacher in Diagon Alley, which Dobby thought was curious... very, very --') deflates the tension into comedy. Mundungus's capture becomes a comic double-act rather than a moment of Harry's righteous fury.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book interrogation scene is one of Mundungus's most significant appearances — it is where Harry finally confronts him with real anger, where his moral shabbiness is laid bare, and where the crucial locket intelligence is extracted under duress. The film's injection of Dobby's comedy routine repositions the scene as light entertainment, softening what the book frames as a confrontation with a genuinely contemptible figure. Mundungus's shabbiness is played for laughs rather than as a character indictment.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (Grimmauld Place kitchen interrogation) — Mundungus not physically confronted by Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 197-213: Harry drops to his knees beside Mundungus, points his wand deliberately at his nose, and drives the interrogation with intensity and personal anger. Kreacher attacks Mundungus with a saucepan. Harry explicitly tells Kreacher 'if he needs persuading, you can do the honours.' The scene is one of Harry's most assertive moments against someone he despises.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's interrogation is abbreviated and less physically confrontational. Harry asks about the locket without the same sustained wand-to-nose intensity or the saucepan assault. The scene moves quickly to Mundungus identifying Umbridge via the newspaper photo.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Harry's agency in the book scene — personally dominating and extracting information from someone who wronged him and Sirius — is a meaningful character beat showing Harry's determination and righteous anger. The film reduces this to a functional information exchange, losing the personal dimension of Harry confronting the man who plundered his godfather's belongings.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (Diagon Alley montage) — Mundungus depicted with 'cruel smile'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus does not characterise Mundungus as cruel — he is greedy, cowardly, and morally flexible, but his villainy is petty and self-serving rather than malicious. Book Scene 52 even shows him capable of self-aware humour ('Will nicked 'em orf Warty Harris in the first place so I wasn't really doing nothing wrong').
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5's stage direction describes Mundungus concluding a transaction 'with a cruel smile,' framing him as predatory and sinister rather than a bumbling opportunist.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While this is a minor visual beat, characterising Mundungus as cruel rather than cowardly and self-interested misrepresents the book's version of him. His function in the narrative depends on him being a morally compromised but essentially small-time figure — not a villain with malicious intent. The 'cruel smile' nudges him toward a different register.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (Aberforth scene, Deathly Hallows Part 2) — Mundungus mentioned as seller of the mirror shard
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book corpus (Scenes 230-233) reveals the most significant dimension of Mundungus's arc: he was Confunded by Snape on Dumbledore's instructions to suggest the decoy-Harrys plan, meaning his role in the Seven Potters mission was orchestrated as part of Dumbledore's larger design. This gives Mundungus a covert structural importance entirely absent from his bumbling surface persona.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Mundungus is mentioned only as the seller of the mirror shard to Aberforth ('Mundungus Fletcher, 'bout a year ago'). The Confundus/Snape dimension of his character is not present in the film corpus at all.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's revelation that Mundungus was unknowingly manipulated by Snape/Dumbledore retroactively recontextualises his entire role: the decoy plan that defined the Seven Potters mission was seeded through him. This adds a layer of tragic complexity — the bumbling coward was a tool of the grand design. The film reduces him purely to a petty thief and coward with no hidden structural significance, losing one of the more quietly affecting pieces of Dumbledore's chess game.
